web/interpretation_state.py:R5:_validate:
R5 `isinstance(source_field, str)`. This function IS the honest Tier-3 parse for one item of `node.options['mapping']` — an untyped `Mapping[str, Any]` persisted on a field_mapper composer node and round-tripped through sessions.db storage, a composer LLM tool call, or YAML import. Both parameters are annotated `object` deliberately: nothing upstream has narrowed them, and the function's whole job is to refuse a non-str and construct the owned `tuple[str, str]` it returns — ADR-032's 'parse what ELSPETH does not own, construct an owned type', with the raise, not a default, on the malformed path.

WHY NOT @trust_boundary. The decorator binds exactly ONE `source_param` (`contracts/trust_boundary.py::trust_boundary` inspects the signature at decoration time and requires the name to be a real parameter), but the two flagged operands are two SEPARATE parameters, `source_field` and `target_field`. A decorator naming either one leaves the other finding standing and misdescribes the boundary. Collapsing the signature into a single tuple parameter purely to fit the decorator's one-slot mechanism would be shaping the code around the gate, which this project forbids.

WHY isinstance AND NOT `type(x) is str`. The sole caller is the raw-html cleanup arm of `validate_pipeline_decision_semantics`, which feeds the returned names into `_looks_like_raw_html_field` and a membership test against `web_scrape_raw_fields`. A `str` SUBCLASS is a legitimate field name arriving from YAML import or a composer tool call; the exact-type form would divert it into the ValueError arm and reject a well-formed pipeline. This is the else-branch-is-a-failure-path case that docs/agents/recent-code-hints.md (2026-08-29) names as NOT a drop-in for the exact-type idiom.

WHAT IT PROTECTS. The raw-html cleanup review contract. If a malformed pair were coerced or silently skipped, a field_mapper could be credited with dropping the upstream web_scrape's raw content/fingerprint fields it does not actually drop, and the pipeline_decision review card minted by `_raw_html_cleanup_artifact_hash` would bind an artifact hash to a mapping the runtime will not honour. Raising routes the state back to the composer as a contract error instead.

R5 `isinstance(target_field, str)` — the second operand of the same single guard as `.../test/values[0]/operand`, in the same function, protecting the same invariant. See that key's rationale in full: `_validated_mapping_pair` is the honest Tier-3 parse of one `node.options['mapping']` item, it raises ValueError rather than defaulting, and it returns the owned `tuple[str, str]`. This operand is flagged separately only because the rule reports each `isinstance` call in the `or` expression. The target-field half matters on its own: `_preserved_mapping_fields` and the caller's preserved-field set are keyed on BOTH sides of each mapping entry, so a non-str target would otherwise reach `_looks_like_raw_html_field` and the `web_scrape_raw_fields` membership test as an un-stripped non-string.
web/app.py:R6:_periodic_orphan_cleanup:a:
R6 `except (SQLAlchemyError, OSError, SchemaCompatibilityError) as cleanup_exc`. Not a swallow: this is the retry boundary of an unbounded background sweeper, and the catch is already narrowed to exactly the recoverable audit/IO classes.

CONTROL, BY SYMBOL. (1) The exception tuple itself is the control: `SQLAlchemyError` covers DB-layer transients raised out of `session_service.cancel_all_orphaned_runs` / `cancel_all_orphaned_run_records` (engine.begin(), conn.execute()), `OSError` covers SQLite file-level failures that escape before SQLAlchemy wraps them, and `SchemaCompatibilityError` covers a Landscape schema skew reached through `_reconcile_pending_landscape_runs`. Programmer-bug classes are NOT caught — an `AttributeError` from a drifted `ExecutionServiceImpl` attribute, a `TypeError` from a signature change, or an `AssertionError` from an invariant guard propagates out of the `while True` and terminates the task. (2) That termination is not silent: `_service_lifespan` holds the task as `orphan_task` and its `finally` block awaits it under `contextlib.suppress(asyncio.CancelledError)`, which is narrowed to cancellation ONLY — so a stored non-cancel exception re-raises at shutdown and reaches the operator. That await is the sibling R7 site in this same bucket, and it is the mechanism that makes this narrow catch safe rather than terminal.

WHAT IT PROTECTS AND WHY NOT RAISE. Raising here would kill the sweeper on the first DB transient, and the sweeper is the only thing that reclaims runs orphaned by SIGKILL/OOM DURING uptime; a permanently blocked session (partial unique index on active runs) is the failure this loop exists to prevent. `telemetry.orphaned_runs_cancelled_total` is credited only from what `cancel_all_orphaned_runs` / `cancel_all_orphaned_run_records` actually returned: when the cancel step itself fails, `cancelled` is still 0 and nothing is credited; when the cancel succeeded and the subsequent `_reconcile_pending_landscape_runs` raised, the counter is credited with exactly the runs that really were cancelled, whose reconciliation the `LANDSCAPE_RECONCILIATION_PENDING_SUFFIX` reason marks for retry. Either way the counter never claims work that did not happen, and the next interval retries. `exc_info` is deliberately omitted from `slog.error('periodic_orphan_cleanup_failed', exc_class=...)`: SQLAlchemyError `__cause__` chains routinely carry the DB connection URL, schema names, and the sqlite file path.
web/app.py:R6:_service_lifespan:ast=body:
R6 `except (SQLAlchemyError, OSError, SchemaCompatibilityError) as cleanup_exc` on the STARTUP orphan sweep. Same narrow tuple and same reasoning as the periodic sweeper, but the control that makes it correct here is a deliberate contrast drawn three statements above it.

CONTROL, BY SYMBOL. `app.state.blob_service.reconcile_inline_custody_publications()` runs IMMEDIATELY before this try and is deliberately NOT wrapped — its comment states the rule: inline custody stages are part of the blob integrity protocol, so the server must not serve until every stage has a row-authoritative outcome. A failure there propagates and aborts lifespan startup. Orphan-run bookkeeping is explicitly the other category: best-effort, idempotent, and retried. So the boundary between fail-closed and absorb is drawn by which call sits inside the try, and the integrity-bearing one sits outside it.

RECOVERY IS PROVEN, NOT ASSUMED. `_periodic_orphan_cleanup` is started later in this same function with `interval_seconds=settings.orphan_run_check_interval_seconds` and performs the identical `cancel_all_orphaned_run_records` + `_reconcile_pending_landscape_runs` work, so a startup failure is re-attempted within one interval rather than lost. `app.state.sessions_telemetry.orphaned_runs_cancelled_total` is credited only from what `cancel_all_orphaned_run_records` actually returned: if the cancel step itself failed, `cancelled_runs` is still the empty list bound before the try and nothing is credited; if the cancel succeeded and the subsequent `_reconcile_pending_landscape_runs` raised, the counter is credited with exactly the runs that really were cancelled, whose reconciliation the `LANDSCAPE_RECONCILIATION_PENDING_SUFFIX` reason marks for the periodic sweeper to retry. The counter never claims work that did not happen. `slog.error('lifespan_orphan_cleanup_failed', exc_class=...)` records the class without `exc_info`, for the same credential-bearing-`__cause__` reason as the periodic site.

R6 `except TimeoutError` around the composer boot config probe. This is the one absorbed class in a handler chain whose every other arm re-raises.

CONTROL, BY SYMBOL. Three sibling handlers on the SAME try each end in a bare `raise`: `except ComposerBootConfigError: probe_status = 'rejected'; raise` (a real misconfiguration still fail-closes and aborts boot), `except asyncio.CancelledError: probe_status = 'cancelled'; raise` (shutdown is never masked), and `except Exception: probe_status = 'local_error'; raise` (anything unanticipated, including a programmer bug in `probe_composer_config`, still terminates startup). TimeoutError is therefore not a catch-all remnant — it is the single named class the boot contract absorbs. The `finally` block is the second control: it writes `attributes['probe_status'] = probe_status` and records `_COMPOSER_BOOT_CONFIG_COUNTER.add(1, attributes)` and `_COMPOSER_BOOT_CONFIG_PROBE_LATENCY.record(...)` on EVERY path, so the timeout is durably visible as `transient_failure` in operator telemetry rather than disappearing.

WHAT IT PROTECTS. The probe is a reachability check bounded by `_COMPOSER_BOOT_PROBE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` via `asyncio.wait_for`, not an admission gate. Treating a slow or briefly unreachable provider as fatal would make web-process startup depend on a third-party endpoint's latency; the composer's LLM calls are exercised at first use, where a genuine provider failure surfaces against a real request. The logged warning states exactly that (`action='booting; composer LLM calls will be exercised at first use'`). Absorbing the timeout does not weaken any composer invariant: no pipeline structure is authored here, and `provider='server'` is not involved — this call only asks whether the configured model/endpoint answers.
web/app.py:R7:_service_lifespan:ast=body:
R7 `with contextlib.suppress(asyncio.CancelledError): await orphan_task`. The suppressed exception is the cancellation THIS code requested on the immediately preceding line.

CONTROL, BY SYMBOL. `orphan_task.cancel()` runs one statement earlier in the same `finally`. Awaiting a cancelled task is the required way to join it, and that await necessarily re-raises the `asyncio.CancelledError` the cancel just injected; suppressing it is the documented asyncio idiom for shutdown, not error hiding. The suppression is narrowed to `asyncio.CancelledError` EXACTLY — not `Exception`, not `BaseException` — so any OTHER exception stored on the task re-raises out of this `finally` and fails lifespan shutdown loudly. That is precisely the escape route that makes the sibling R6 narrow catch in `_periodic_orphan_cleanup` safe: the programmer-bug classes that handler deliberately does not absorb kill the task, and this await is where they surface to the operator.

WHAT IT PROTECTS. Ordering. The cancel-and-join happens before `app.state.readiness_probe_runner.close()`, `execution_service.shutdown()`, `app.state.operator_telemetry.shutdown()` and the engine teardown, so the sweeper cannot race a query against a disposed pool or write a terminal state after the executor has drained. Replacing the suppress with a re-raise would abort that ordered teardown on every normal shutdown.
web/app.py:R6:_frontend_build_identity:a:
R6 `except OSError: return None` when reading the built SPA `index.html`. `None` is not a swallowed failure here — it is a declared value of the function's `str | None` return type, and it is the value that DISARMS the feature.

CONTROL, BY SYMBOL. The result is assigned once at startup to `app.state.frontend_build` and published only as the `'frontend_build'` field of the `/api/system/status` payload. The consumer is the SPA deploy beacon: `web/frontend/src/types/index.ts` types the field `frontend_build?: string | null`, and `web/frontend/src/App.tsx` requires a STABLE mismatch across `STALE_BUILD_POLLS_REQUIRED` polls before it offers a refresh. A null therefore cannot produce a false 'your tab is stale' prompt — it simply means the client never arms the comparison. That null path is the same one taken when the regex finds no hashed entry asset, which is the ordinary dev/test deployment shape.

WHY NOT RESTRUCTURE. A pre-check (`index_html.is_file()`) plus an unguarded `read_text` would convert an IO or permission error on a purely cosmetic cache-coherence beacon into a hard web-process boot failure, and would still be racy. Narrowing to `except FileNotFoundError` does not clear the finding either — R6 fires on any specific exception whose handler returns a default (`_is_default_return_value` treats `None` as a silent default regardless of the class caught), so narrowing buys a behaviour change and no reduction. Nothing audited, nothing transactional, and no admission decision reads `app.state.frontend_build`.
web/app.py:R4:_create_app:_log_correlati:
R4 `except Exception: return` inside `_log_correlation_warning`. The broad arm is the SECOND handler, and the first one is the control.

CONTROL, BY SYMBOL. `except contract_errors.TIER_1_ERRORS: raise` precedes it on the same try. Registered Tier-1 framework/audit failures therefore remain fail-closed and escape this helper unchanged, matching the canonical engine best-effort boundary; the broad arm below it can only ever absorb an ordinary logging-backend failure. Handler order is load-bearing here, and reversing the two arms would silence Tier-1 — this is the same ordering rule docs/agents/recent-code-hints.md records for `except IntegrityError: raise` preceding a broad handler (2026-08-26).

WHAT IT PROTECTS. This helper emits bounded lookup evidence (`event`, `status_code`, `request_id`) ALONGSIDE an HTTP error response that has already been classified and redacted by the app-level exception handler that calls it. The response is the primary outcome; the log line is the recovery channel of last resort. Letting a structlog/handler failure propagate would convert a deterministic, redacted 4xx into an unrelated 500 — turning a logging defect into a wrong answer to the client and destroying the correlation id the caller was trying to record. There is also no safe secondary logger with which to report an ordinary failure of the logger, so a re-raise has no recipient. The bare `return` is the whole handler body: nothing is retried, defaulted, or fabricated.
web/app.py:R4:_create_app:_prometheus_me:
R4 `except Exception as scrape_exc` around `generate_latest()`. There IS an explicit error path here; R4 fires on structure, not on absence of one.

WHY THE RULE FIRES ANYWAY. `TierModelVisitor._check_exception_handler` clears a BROAD handler only when `iter_own_scope` finds an `ast.Raise` in it. Unlike the R6 branch it never consults `_is_default_return_value`, so an explicit non-default `return` cannot clear an R4 the way it clears an R6. This handler returns `Response(content=b'# scrape failed\n', status_code=503, media_type=CONTENT_TYPE_LATEST, headers=_METRICS_NO_STORE_HEADERS)` — a bounded, deterministic, content-free error response — and logs `_handler_slog.error('prometheus_scrape_failed', exc_class=..., detail=str(scrape_exc)[:200])`. Nothing is absorbed silently.

WHY BROAD AND NOT NARROW. `generate_latest()` walks the global Prometheus `REGISTRY` and executes every registered collector's `collect()`, including third-party ones; the exception classes reachable through that fan-out are not enumerable by this module. Re-raising is the harmful option: Starlette's default 500 handler would render the traceback into the scrape response BODY, which is exactly the internal-detail leak this endpoint must not have. A 503 also matches scraper semantics — Prometheus retries it gracefully rather than recording a hard failure.

WHY THE BOUNDED MESSAGE IS SAFE HERE. Unlike the secret-bearing DB exception sites elsewhere in this file (which log `exc_class` only), the route has ALREADY authenticated before collection — the bearer scheme check plus `hmac.compare_digest(candidate, expected)` above — and the 200-character `detail` identifies which collector broke without reading any request-controlled input. Audit-primacy: this endpoint reads in-memory counter state only, so a failure is a telemetry-system (operational) failure, logged and not audited; no Landscape record is written or withheld on this path.
